title: Waves: motion, interference and standing patterns
voiceInstructions: Warm, engaging female teacher with a natural General American English accent. Relaxed, welcoming and lightly playful, with a gentle smile and conversational rhythm. Keep scientific terms precise and avoid an announcer cadence. Slow down for equations, numbers and conversions. Give brief natural thinking pauses after questions. Do not add words or laughter absent from the script.

sources.title: NTA: Official JEE Main 2026 syllabus, Physics Unit 10

chapters.title: A disturbance travels; particles oscillate
chapters.formula: vwave = f lambda = omega/k; y = A sin(kx - omega t + phi)
points: Transverse oscillation is perpendicular to propagation; longitudinal oscillation is parallel.
A wave equation describes both position along the medium and time.
Wave speed and the velocity of an individual particle are different quantities.
chapters.script: Hey, welcome back. Imagine sending a small pulse along a stretched rope. The pulse travels toward your friend, but a little mark on the rope moves up and down, not all the way to your friend. That's our first distinction: the disturbance travels while the material oscillates locally. Mechanical waves need a medium. In a transverse wave, particle motion is perpendicular to propagation. In a longitudinal wave, such as sound in air, it is parallel, producing compressions and rarefactions. For a sinusoidal wave, wavelength is the spacing between neighboring points with the same phase, such as two crests. Frequency counts oscillations per second. In one period the pattern advances one wavelength, so wave speed equals frequency times wavelength. We can write displacement as amplitude times sine of k x minus omega t plus phase. Here k equals two pi divided by wavelength, and omega equals two pi times frequency. Holding phase constant shows that this minus-sign form travels in the positive x direction. With a plus sign before omega t, it travels in the negative direction. Take wavelength half a meter and frequency forty hertz. The pattern moves at twenty meters per second. That is not the speed of a marked particle. Particle velocity comes from differentiating displacement with respect to time at a fixed position. In JEE, identify which velocity the question actually asks for before touching a formula.

chapters.title: What sets speed on a stretched string?
points: The ideal string model assumes small transverse disturbances and uniform tension.
Higher tension increases speed; greater mass per unit length decreases it.
For a fixed medium, changing source frequency changes wavelength rather than speed.
chapters.script: Why does a tighter rope transmit a disturbance faster? Tension supplies the restoring influence that pulls neighboring parts into motion. Greater mass per unit length means more inertia. For small transverse waves on an ideal uniform string, speed is the square root of tension divided by mass per unit length. We use mu for that linear mass density, measured in kilograms per meter. Do not substitute volume density here. Suppose a two meter string has mass four grams and tension eight newtons. Convert four grams to zero point zero zero four kilograms. Divide by two meters: mu is zero point zero zero two kilograms per meter. The wave speed is the square root of four thousand, about sixty three point two meters per second. If tension becomes four times larger while mu stays fixed, predict the new speed. Pause for a moment. The square root makes the speed twice as large. Now imagine changing only the driving frequency. With the same string and tension, wave speed remains the same in this ideal model. Since speed equals frequency times wavelength, doubling frequency halves wavelength. That's a very useful consistency check. On a different medium the wavelength may change, but a wave transmitted across a stationary boundary retains the driving frequency. The particles and restoring forces determine the propagation speed; the source sets the frequency.

chapters.title: Superposition and reflection
chapters.formula: yresult = y1 + y2; equal amplitudes: Aresult = 2A |cos(delta phi/2)|
points: For linear waves, add displacements with their signs at the same place and time.
Equal coherent waves reinforce in phase and cancel in opposite phase.
An ideal fixed string end inverts reflected displacement; a free end does not.
chapters.script: Two pulses meet on a rope. Do they collide like two solid objects? In the linear wave model, no. Their displacements add while they overlap, and then the pulses continue. That is superposition. Add signed displacements at the same position and time, not just the positive heights drawn on a page. A displacement of three centimeters upward combined with two centimeters downward gives one centimeter upward. For two coherent sinusoidal waves of the same frequency, with equal amplitude A and constant phase difference, the resultant amplitude is twice A times the absolute value of cosine of half the phase difference. In phase, they reinforce; opposite in phase, they cancel. With each amplitude two centimeters and a phase difference of one hundred and twenty degrees, the resultant amplitude is two centimeters, not four. Here cancellation means a local resultant displacement pattern; it does not mean energy simply disappears from the entire wave system. Now reflect a pulse from an ideal fixed end of a string. The end cannot move, so the reflected displacement pulse is inverted. At an ideal free end it reflects without displacement inversion. These statements concern transverse string displacement, not a universal rule for every pressure wave or boundary. Incident and reflected waves can repeatedly overlap. If their frequency, amplitude and boundary conditions match appropriately, that overlap creates the standing patterns we'll study next.

chapters.title: Standing waves on a fixed string
chapters.formula: y = 2A sin(kx) cos(omega t); lambda_n = 2L/n; f_n = n v/(2L)
points: Nodes remain at zero displacement; antinodes have the largest oscillation amplitude.
Neighboring nodes are half a wavelength apart; node to nearest antinode is a quarter wavelength.
A string fixed at both ends has all integer harmonics in the ideal model.
chapters.script: Combine two identical sinusoidal waves traveling in opposite directions. Their sum can be written as twice A times sine of k x times cosine of omega t, after choosing a suitable phase origin. Notice the separation: position determines the local amplitude, while time makes each point oscillate. The pattern doesn't march along the string. Nodes stay at zero displacement; antinodes have the greatest amplitude. Adjacent nodes are half a wavelength apart, and a node to its nearest antinode is a quarter wavelength. For a string fixed at both ends, both ends must be nodes. Its length must fit an integer number of half wavelengths. That gives wavelength two L divided by n, and frequency n times wave speed divided by two L. The first harmonic is the fundamental. On this string the second harmonic is the first overtone, and the third harmonic is the second overtone. Let's use length one meter and speed one hundred meters per second. The fundamental is fifty hertz. At the third harmonic, frequency is one hundred and fifty hertz and wavelength is two thirds of a meter. There are three loops, four nodes including the endpoints, and three antinodes. Don't count loops as nodes. An ideal standing wave formed by equal opposite traveling waves has no net time-averaged energy transport along the string, unlike either traveling wave on its own.

chapters.title: Air columns, harmonics and beats
chapters.formula: open-open: f_n = n v/(2L); closed-open: f_n = n v/(4L), n = 1,3,5; fbeat = |f1 - f2|
points: In ideal air columns, open ends are displacement antinodes; closed ends are displacement nodes.
A closed-open pipe supports odd harmonics; its first overtone is the third harmonic.
Close frequencies produce beats at their absolute frequency difference.
chapters.script: Let's move from a string to air in a pipe. Sound is longitudinal. An ideal open end is a displacement antinode and approximately a pressure node. A closed end is a displacement node and a pressure antinode. Keep the quantity straight: pressure and displacement have opposite node patterns. Ignoring end correction, an open pipe at both ends fits half wavelengths and has all integer harmonics. A pipe closed at one end and open at the other fits an odd number of quarter wavelengths, so only odd harmonics occur. Its first overtone is the third harmonic, not the second. For length half a meter and sound speed three hundred and forty meters per second, a closed-open pipe has fundamental one hundred and seventy hertz. Its first overtone is five hundred and ten hertz. Real open ends require an effective-length correction, so use it if the question supplies one. Finally, hear two tones of two hundred and fifty six and two hundred and sixty hertz together. Their relative phase changes slowly, causing alternating reinforcement and weakening. You hear four beats per second: the absolute frequency difference. Beats are easiest to notice for nearby frequencies and comparable amplitudes. Unequal amplitudes need not produce complete silence at the minima. To solve JEE wave problems, first name the wave quantity and boundary conditions, then choose the relation. A correct picture prevents far more errors than a longer formula list.

quiz.question: A wave has wavelength 0.5 m and frequency 40 Hz. Its propagation speed is:
A uniform 2 m string has mass 4 g and tension 8 N. Ideal transverse wave speed is approximately:
Two coherent waves each have amplitude 2 cm and phase difference 120 degrees. Resultant amplitude is:
A 1 m string fixed at both ends has wave speed 100 m/s. Its third-harmonic frequency is:
An ideal closed-open pipe of length 0.5 m has sound speed 340 m/s. Its first overtone is:
quiz.explanation: Fundamental is v/(4L) = 170 Hz. First overtone is the third harmonic: 510 Hz.
